danish.title: Første epilog (1813–20) — Kapitel 15
paragraphs: Samtalen ved aftensmaden drejede sig ikke om politik eller selskaber, men handlede om det emne, Nikolaj bedst kunne lide — minder fra 1812. Denisov bragte dem på bane, og Pierre var særlig elskværdig og underholdende om dem. Familien skiltes i den bedste forståelse.

Efter aftensmaden gik Nikolaj, der havde klædt sig om i sit arbejdsværelse og givet instrukser til forvalteren, der havde ventet på ham, ind i soveværelset i sin slobrok, hvor han fandt sin hustru stadig ved sit bord, skrivende.
»Hvad skriver du, Marja?« spurgte Nikolaj.
Grevinde Marja rødmede. Hun var bange for, at det, hun skrev, ikke ville blive forstået eller godkendt af sin mand.
Hun havde villet skjule det for ham, men var samtidig glad for, at han havde overrasket hende ved det, og at hun nu måtte fortælle ham det.
»En dagbog, Nikolaj,« svarede hun og rakte ham et blåt hæfte fyldt med hendes faste, kraftige håndskrift.
»En dagbog?« gentog Nikolaj med et anstrøg af ironi og tog hæftet op.
Det var på fransk.

Den 4. december. I dag, da Andrusha (hendes ældste dreng) vågnede, ville han ikke klæde sig på, og mademoiselle Louise sendte bud efter mig. Han var uartig og stædig. Jeg prøvede med trusler, men han blev blot vred. Så tog jeg sagen i egen hånd: jeg lod ham alene og begyndte med ammens hjælp at gøre de andre børn i stand, idet jeg fortalte ham, at jeg ikke elskede ham. I lang tid var han tavs, som om han var forbavset, derefter sprang han ud af sengen, løb hen til mig i sin skjorte og hulkede, så jeg ikke kunne berolige ham i lang tid. Det var tydeligt, at det, der plagede ham mest, var, at han havde bedrøvet mig. Bagefter om aftenen, da jeg gav ham hans mærkat, begyndte han igen at græde ynkeligt og kysse mig. Man kan gøre alt med ham gennem ømhed.
»Hvad er et 'mærkat'?« spurgte Nikolaj.
»Jeg er begyndt at give de ældste karakterer hver aften, der viser, hvordan de har opført sig.«

Nikolaj så ind i de strålende øjne, der betragtede ham, og fortsatte med at bladre og læse. I dagbogen var nedskrevet alt i børnenes liv, som forekom deres mor at vise noget om deres karakter eller give anledning til almene tanker om opdragelsesmetoder. Det var for størstedelen ganske ubetydelige småting, men forekom hverken moderen eller faderen ubetydelige, nu da han for første gang læste denne dagbog om sine børn.
Under datoen den 5. stod:

Mitja var uartig ved bordet. Far sagde, at han ikke måtte få dessert. Han fik ingen, men så så ulykkeligt og grådigt på de andre, mens de spiste! Jeg tror, at straf ved at fratage børn søde sager kun udvikler deres grådighed. Må fortælle Nikolaj dette.

Nikolaj lagde bogen fra sig og så på sin hustru. De strålende øjne betragtede ham spørgende: ville han billige eller misbillige hendes dagbog? Der kunne ingen tvivl være, ikke blot om hans billigelse, men også om hans beundring for sin hustru.

Måske behøver det ikke gøres så pedantisk, tænkte Nikolaj, eller overhovedet ikke gøres, men denne utrættelige, vedvarende åndelige indsats, hvis eneste mål var børnenes moralske vel, henrykte ham. Havde Nikolaj kunnet analysere sine følelser, ville han have fundet, at hans faste, ømme og stolte kærlighed til sin hustru beroede på hans følelse af undren over hendes åndelighed og over den ophøjede moralske verden, næsten uden for hans rækkevidde, hvori hun levede.

Han var stolt af hendes klogskab og godhed, erkendte sin egen ubetydelighed ved siden af hende i den åndelige verden og glædede sig så meget desto mere over, at hun med en sådan sjæl ikke blot tilhørte ham, men var en del af ham selv.

»Jeg billiger det fuldt ud, min kæreste!« sagde han med et betegnende blik, og efter en kort pause tilføjede han: »Og jeg opførte mig dårligt i dag. Du var ikke i arbejdsværelset. Vi begyndte at skændes — Pierre og jeg — og jeg mistede besindelsen. Men han er umulig: som et barn! Jeg ved ikke, hvad der ville blive af ham, hvis Natasja ikke holdt ham i tøjlerne... Har du nogen idé om, hvorfor han rejste til Petersborg? De har dannet...«
»Ja, jeg ved det,« sagde grevinde Marja. »Natasja fortalte mig det.«

»Nå, så ved du det,« fortsatte Nikolaj, der blev varm alene ved mindet om deres diskussion, »han ville overbevise mig om, at det er enhver ærlig mands pligt at gå imod regeringen, og at troskabseden og pligten... Jeg er ked af, du ikke var der. De faldt alle over mig — Denisov og Natasja... Natasja er absurd. Hvor hun hersker over ham! Og dog behøver der blot komme en diskussion, og hun har ingen egne ord, men gentager bare hans udsagn...« tilføjede Nikolaj og gav efter for den uimodståelige tilbøjelighed, der frister os til at dømme dem, der står os nærmest. Han glemte, at det, han sagde om Natasja, ord til andet kunne siges om ham selv i forhold til sin hustru.
»Ja, det har jeg bemærket,« sagde grevinde Marja.
»Da jeg fortalte ham, at pligten og eden står over alt, gav han sig til at bevise Gud ved hvad! Synd du ikke var der — hvad ville du have sagt?«

»Som jeg ser det, havde du ganske ret, og det sagde jeg til Natasja. Pierre siger, at alle lider, pines og fordærves, og at det er vores pligt at hjælpe vores næste. Selvfølgelig har han ret deri,« sagde grevinde Marja, »men han glemmer, at vi har andre pligter tættere på os, pligter, som Gud selv har anvist os, og at vi, skønt vi måtte udsætte os selv for fare, ikke må bringe vores børn i fare.«

»Ja, det er det! Det var netop, hvad jeg sagde til ham,« faldt Nikolaj ind, som troede, at han virkelig havde sagt det. »Men de insisterede på deres eget synspunkt: kærlighed til næsten og kristendom — og alt dette i den unge Nikolajs nærværelse, som var gået ind i mit arbejdsværelse og slog alle mine ting i stykker.«

»Åh, Nikolaj, ved du, at jeg ofte er bekymret for lille Nikolaj,« sagde grevinde Marja. »Han er en så enestående dreng. Jeg er bange for, at jeg forsømmer ham til fordel for mine egne: vi har alle børn og slægtninge, mens han ikke har nogen. Han er bestandig alene med sine tanker.«

»Jamen, jeg synes ikke, du behøver at bebrejde dig noget på hans vegne. Alt, hvad den mest kærlige mor kan gøre for sin søn, har du gjort og gør for ham, og det er jeg naturligvis glad for. Han er en fin dreng, en fin dreng! I aften lyttede han til Pierre i en slags transe, og tænk — da vi gik ind til aftensmad, kiggede jeg, og han havde slået alt i stykker på mit bord, og han fortalte mig det selv med det samme! Jeg har aldrig kendt ham til at lyve. En fin dreng, en fin dreng!« gentog Nikolaj, der i sit hjerte ikke var glad for Nikolaj Bolkonskij, men altid var ivrig efter at anerkende, at han var en fin dreng.

»Alligevel er jeg ikke det samme som hans egen mor,« sagde grevinde Marja. »Jeg føler, at jeg ikke er det samme, og det plager mig. En vidunderlig dreng, men jeg er forfærdeligt bange for ham. Det ville være godt for ham at have kammerater.«

»Nå, det varer ikke længe. Næste sommer tager jeg ham med til Petersborg,« sagde Nikolaj. »Ja, Pierre har altid været en drømmer og vil altid være det,« fortsatte han og vendte tilbage til samtalen i arbejdsværelset, som tydeligvis havde forstyrret ham. »Jamen, hvad vedkommer det mig, hvad der foregår dér — om Araktjejev er slem, og alt det? Hvad vedkom det mig, dengang jeg giftede mig og var så dybt i gæld, at jeg truedes med fængsel, og havde en mor, der ikke kunne se eller forstå det? Og så er der dig og børnene og vores anliggender. Er det for min egen fornøjelses skyld, at jeg er på gården eller på kontoret fra morgen til aften? Nej, men jeg ved, at jeg må arbejde for at trøste min mor, for at gengælde dig, og for ikke at efterlade børnene som sådanne stakler, som jeg selv var.«

Grevinde Marja ville fortælle ham, at mennesket ikke lever af brød alene, og at han lagde for stor vægt på disse ting. Men hun vidste, at hun ikke måtte sige det, og at det ville være nytteløst. Hun tog blot hans hånd og kyssede den. Han opfattede det som et tegn på billigelse og en bekræftelse af sine tanker, og efter nogle minutters eftertanke fortsatte han med at tænke højt.
»Ved du, Marja, i dag kom Elias Mitrofanych« (det var hans forvalter) »tilbage fra godset i Tambov og fortalte mig, at de allerede byder firs tusind rubler for skoven.«
Og med et ivrigt ansigt begyndte Nikolaj at tale om muligheden for snart at tilbagekøbe Otradnoje, og tilføjede: »Ti år mere at leve, og jeg efterlader børnene... i en fremragende position.«

Grevinde Marja lyttede til sin mand og forstod alt, hvad han fortalte hende. Hun vidste, at når han tænkte højt på denne måde, spurgte han hende undertiden, hvad han havde sagt, og blev irriteret, hvis han mærkede, at hun havde tænkt på noget andet. Men hun måtte tvinge sig til at være opmærksom, for det, han sagde, interesserede hende slet ikke. Hun så på ham og tænkte ikke, men følte noget helt andet. Hun følte en hengiven, øm kærlighed til denne mand, der aldrig ville forstå alt det, hun forstod, og dette syntes at gøre hendes kærlighed til ham endnu stærkere og tilføjede et drag af lidenskabelig ømhed. Foruden denne følelse, der helt opslugte hende og hindrede hende i at følge detaljerne i sin mands planer, flimrede tanker, der ikke havde nogen forbindelse med det, han sagde, gennem hendes sind. Hun tænkte på sin nevø. Hendes mands beretning om drengens ophidselse, mens Pierre talte, havde slået hende stærkt, og forskellige træk af hans milde, følsomme karakter dukkede op i hendes sind; og mens hun tænkte på sin nevø, tænkte hun også på sine egne børn. Hun sammenlignede dem ikke med ham, men sammenlignede sin følelse for dem med sin følelse for ham, og mærkede med beklagelse, at der manglede noget i hendes følelse for den unge Nikolaj.

Undertiden forekom det hende, at denne forskel skyldtes aldersforskellen, men hun følte sig skyldig over for ham og lovede i sit hjerte at gøre det bedre og udføre det umulige — i dette liv at elske sin mand, sine børn, lille Nikolaj og alle sine næste, som Kristus elskede menneskeheden. Grevinde Marjas sjæl stræbte altid mod det uendelige, det evige og det absolutte og kunne derfor aldrig finde ro. Et strengt udtryk af den ophøjede, hemmelige lidelse hos en sjæl, tynget af legemet, viste sig i hendes ansigt. Nikolaj betragtede hende. »Åh Gud! Hvad bliver der af os, hvis hun dør, som jeg altid frygter, når hendes ansigt er sådan?« tænkte han, og idet han stillede sig foran ikonet, begyndte han at sige sine aftenbønner.

english.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: The conversation at supper was not about politics or societies but turned to the subject Nicholas liked best—memories of 1812. Denisov started these, and Pierre was especially engaging and funny about them. The family separated on the friendliest terms.

After supper, Nicholas undressed in his study and gave instructions to the steward who had been waiting for him, then went to the bedroom in his dressing gown, where he found his wife still at her writing desk.
"What are you writing, Mary?" Nicholas asked.
Countess Mary blushed. She was afraid that what she was writing wouldn't be understood or approved by her husband.
She had wanted to hide it from him, but was at the same time glad he had caught her at it and that she would now have to tell him.
"A diary, Nicholas," she replied, handing him a blue exercise book filled with her firm, bold handwriting.
"A diary?" Nicholas repeated with a touch of irony, and took the book.
It was in French.

December 4. Today when Andrusha woke up he didn't want to get dressed, and Mademoiselle Louise sent for me. He was being naughty and stubborn. I tried threats, but he only got angrier. Then I took charge: I left him alone and began helping the nanny get the other children up, telling him I didn't love him. He was quiet for a long time, as if surprised. Then he rushed out to me in his nightshirt and was sobbing so hard that I couldn't calm him down for a long time. He was clearly most upset at having grieved me. Later, when I gave him his report card in the evening, he cried pitifully again as he kissed me. One can do anything with him through kindness.
"What's a 'report card'?" Nicholas asked.
"I've started giving the older children marks every evening, showing how they've behaved."

Nicholas looked into the radiant eyes gazing at him and continued turning pages and reading. Everything that seemed noteworthy about the children's characters or that suggested general principles of child-rearing was recorded in the diary. It was mostly small details, but they did not seem trivial to the mother or to the father who was now reading about his children for the first time.
Under the date "5" was this entry:

Mitya was naughty at the table. Papa said he should have no pudding. He got none, but looked so sadly and hungrily at the others while they ate! I think depriving children of sweets only makes them greedier. Must tell Nicholas.

Nicholas put down the book and looked at his wife. The radiant eyes gazed at him questioningly: would he approve or disapprove of her diary? There could be no doubt—not only of his approval but of his admiration for his wife.

"Perhaps it doesn't need to be done quite so methodically," Nicholas thought, "or even done at all." But this tireless, constant spiritual effort, aimed solely at the children's moral well-being, delighted him. If Nicholas could have analyzed his feelings, he would have found that his proud, tender love for his wife was grounded in this very sense of wonder at her inner life, at the lofty moral world that was almost beyond his reach, in which his wife always lived.

He was proud of her intelligence and goodness, recognized his own insignificance beside her in the spiritual realm, and rejoiced all the more that she—with such a soul—not only belonged to him but was part of himself.

"I completely approve, my dearest!" he said with a meaningful look. After a short pause he added: "And I behaved badly today. You weren't in the study. Pierre and I got into an argument, and I lost my temper. But he's impossible—such a child! I don't know what would happen to him if Natasha didn't keep him in line. Can you imagine what he went to Petersburg for... they're forming—"
"Yes, I know," said Countess Mary. "Natasha told me."

"Well, then you know," Nicholas went on, getting heated again at the mere memory of the discussion, "he wanted to convince me that it's every honest man's duty to go against the government, and that oaths of allegiance and duty... I'm sorry you weren't there. They all ganged up on me—Denisov and Natasha too... Natasha is ridiculous. She's got him completely under her thumb, but when it comes to an argument she has no mind of her own—she just parrots his words," Nicholas added, giving in to his irresistible urge to criticize people he loved. He forgot that what he said about Natasha could just as well be said word for word about himself in relation to his wife.
"Yes, I've noticed that," said Countess Mary.
"When I told him that duty and the oath come above everything, he started trying to prove God knows what! What a shame you weren't there—what would you have said?"

"As I see it, you were quite right, and I told Natasha so. Pierre says that everyone is suffering, being tortured and corrupted, and that it's our duty to help our neighbors. Of course he's right about that," said Countess Mary, "but he forgets that we have other, nearer duties—duties that God himself has set for us—and that we may risk ourselves but not our children."

"Yes, that's exactly what I said to him!" Nicholas put in, genuinely believing he had said it. "But they kept insisting on their view: love of one's neighbor and Christianity—and all this with young Nicholas sitting right there. He had slipped into my study and was smashing things to pieces."

"You know, Nicholas, I'm often worried about young Nicholas," said Countess Mary. "He's such an unusual boy. I'm afraid I neglect him in favor of my own children—we all have our children and our own family ties, while he has no one. He's always alone with his thoughts."

"Well, I don't think you need to blame yourself on his account. Everything the most devoted mother could do for a son, you've done and are doing for him. And of course I'm glad of it. He's a fine boy, a fine boy! This evening he listened to Pierre in a kind of trance. And do you know—when we stood up to go to supper, I looked over and he'd smashed everything on my desk to bits, and he told me about it himself right away. I've never known him to lie. A fine boy, really!" Nicholas repeated, who had no real fondness for young Nicholas Bolkonsky, but was always anxious to acknowledge what a fine boy he was.

"Still, I'm not the same as his own mother," said Countess Mary. "I feel that I'm not, and it troubles me. He's a wonderful boy, but I'm terribly afraid for him. It would be good for him to have companions."

"Well, it won't be for long. Next summer I'll take him to Petersburg," said Nicholas. "Yes, Pierre always was a dreamer and always will be," he went on, returning to the talk in the study, which had clearly upset him. "Well, what business is it of mine what goes on there — whether Arakcheyev is bad, and all that? What business was it of mine when I married and was so deep in debt that I was threatened with prison, and had a mother who could not see or understand it? And then there are you and the children and our affairs. Is it for my own pleasure that I am at the farm or in the office from morning to night? No — I know I must work to comfort my mother, to repay you, and not to leave the children as destitute as I was."

Countess Mary wanted to tell him that man does not live by bread alone, and that he placed too much importance on these things. But she knew she must not say it and that it would be useless. She simply took his hand and kissed it. He took this as a sign of agreement and approval, and after a few moments of silent reflection went on thinking aloud.
"You know, Mary, today Elias Mitrofanych"—his overseer—"came back from the Tambov estate and told me they're already offering eighty thousand for the forest."

And with eager excitement Nicholas began talking about the possibility of buying Otradnoe back before long, adding: "Another ten years of life and I'll leave the children... in an excellent position."

Countess Mary listened to her husband and understood everything he told her. She knew that when he thought aloud like this he would sometimes ask what he'd been saying, and be annoyed if he noticed she'd been thinking about something else. But she had to make a considerable effort to pay attention, because what he said didn't interest her at all. She looked at him and—rather than thinking—felt something else entirely. She felt a submissive, tender love for this man who would never understand everything she understood, and she seemed to love him all the more for that, with a touch of passionate tenderness. This feeling absorbed her and kept her from following the details of his plans. Other thoughts, quite unconnected with what he was saying, flitted through her mind. She thought of her nephew. Her husband’s account of how agitated the boy had been while Pierre was speaking struck her forcibly. She remembered one little trait after another of his gentle, sensitive nature, and from her nephew her thoughts went to her own children. She was not comparing them with him. She was comparing what she felt for them with what she felt for him, and was sorry to find that something was wanting in her love for young Nicholas.

Sometimes it seemed to her that this difference between them came from the difference in their ages, but she also felt herself to be at fault and promised in her heart to do better, to accomplish the impossible—to love her husband, her children, all her relatives, and all people in this life, just as Christ loved mankind. Countess Mary's soul always strived toward the infinite, the eternal, and the absolute, and therefore could never be at peace. A stern expression of the lofty, secret suffering of a soul weighed down by the body appeared on her face. Nicholas looked at her. "My God! What will become of us if she dies, as I always fear when her face looks like that?" he thought, and standing before the icon he began to say his evening prayers.
